title: Partly enciphered Egyptian Coastguard telegram about seized bales of khaki uniforms at Railhead (Western Desert), copy in the Khedive's papers
correspondents: an officer at Railhead (the sender's name is on a sheet not found) to Herbert, 'Sawahil' (Coastguard Administration), Alexandria
place: Railhead (Western Desert railway, Egypt) to Alexandria
shelfmark: Durham University Library, Archives and Special Collections, Abbas Hilmi II papers, HIL/64/890-891 (frame 174 of 234 of the digitised file HIL/64/1-1011, Telegrams Egypt and Sudan: I)
folio_note: Seen as image (1,024 px frame and a 3,075 px stitch of nine region requests). Two Egyptian State Telegraphs forms G 13, telegram no. 30, 129 words, in a clerk's copying hand. Clear English with 17 five-letter cipher groups in three runs: 'the suits are bfefr ptqap rrvtw but have / acpfw msrrx wuuuu rtxsu vtupt vcxwq uzxtr urxrp dvasr rfouu stop uffkfz stswv claimed them but at first denied exact knowledge of contents he gave me the same name of person sending them from Alexandria as you mention namely pmsmp ktvvv who he says is a' (my reading from the image, not collated; the text breaks off, a third sheet was not found). The groups lean heavily on the letters p to x, with runs such as 'wuuuu' and 'ktvvv', so this is not Playfair; it looks like figure groups of a code turned into letters, or a substitution with padding. No decode on the forms.
status: 15 Nov 2026: ciphertext seen; no clear duplicate of this telegram in the frames screened (HIL/64/817-1007 all viewed as cropped contact sheets; HIL/64/1-816 only five frames sampled, so a clear copy may still sit there, as it does for the 1913 Khartoum telegrams in HIL/65). Durham catalogue describes the file only as 'Arabic and code'. known.py: no hit. No literature search beyond that; DECODE not searched (20th-century British traffic is outside it). Not checked: which cipher the Egyptian Coastguard Administration used in 1912, and whether a key survives (TNA FO 141, WO 33; Durham Sudan Archive).
why: A short British field cipher of the Italo-Turkish war period (arms and uniform smuggling to the Ottoman force in Cyrenaica) with rich clear context on both sides of every cipher run; a named sender is hidden in two groups. Small, but the surrounding clear text gives strong cribs.
verify: Find the third sheet and any clear copy in HIL/64/1-816; collate the 17 groups from a full-size stitch; test the system recovered from the HIL/65 cipher/clear pairs.

title: Two partly enciphered Sudan Government telegrams (Phipps to Slatin, Khartoum; Erkowit to Stack), each with a clear copy of the same telegram in the same file
correspondents: P. R. Phipps (Civil Secretary, Khartoum) to R. von Slatin (Inspector-General, then in Cairo); the Governor-General's office at Erkowit ('Hakimam') to L. O. F. Stack (Sudan Agent, Cairo)
shelfmark: Durham University Library, Archives and Special Collections, Abbas Hilmi II papers, HIL/65/157-158 (cipher) with HIL/65/159-160 (the same telegram, no. 499, in clear); HIL/65/148 (cipher) with HIL/65/153 (the same telegram, no. 286, in clear). Frames 42-44 of 312 of the digitised file HIL/65/1-1127, Telegrams Egypt and Sudan II
folio_note: Seen as image (3,074 px stitch of frame HIL/65/153-158; 2,049 px stitches of the frames before and after). No. 499, Khartoum 12 May 1913, 107 words: clear English with 24 five-letter groups in three runs, 'we cannot Tfwax fozzy xomsv fzwuv socht consequently hope you will agree cswfw zjdls jjzjs zwnwd lwgov durxd njdls vlvsz wsxns xobss as it would not be fair ...' and 'to send him Gwzvg wnjkd nxsoj grwdj degvp xwmrv lvsdx eznxp xfqxs if we cannot find another' (my reading, not collated). The clear copy HIL/65/159-160 gives the same passages as 'we cannot move Matthew from Tokar consequently hope you will agree promotion Wills to Dongola and sending Sagar to Red Sea as it would not be fair ...' and 'to send him to Talodi under Wilson in place of Sagar next December if we cannot find'. No. 286, Erkowit 16 May 1913, 221 words: one run of about 49 letters, 'cmuvl bgtmx blebn ltfuznugs gwuyt hutni xtgxn sxomlybngf', where the clear copy HIL/65/153 has 'Hewson has just inspected government land at Bagtir stop'. Cipher is about 5 to 25 per cent longer than the clear text.
status: 15 Nov 2026: NOT undeciphered in the strict sense: the file itself holds a clear copy of both telegrams, so the plaintext is known and only the key is missing. Recorded because it is ciphertext with adjacent plaintext (a key-recovery case) and because the recovered system may bear on HIL/64/890-891. Durham's catalogue names only 'partially encoded message from Phipps to Slatin (HIL/65/157-158)'; the pairing with the clear copies is this sweep's observation. System not identified: the first mapping tried by eye (o+m to 'wf', o+t to 'wz') fits a digraphic cipher such as Playfair but was not tested. known.py: no hit beyond the first Arabic sweep's note that the file was not viewed. No literature search.
why: A clean cipher-with-crib pair from the Sudan Government's own traffic in 1913, copied for the Khedive's intelligence service: the names of officials being moved are what was hidden. Key recovery from the adjacent plaintext should be quick and would show which cipher Khartoum used a year before the war.
verify: Collate cipher against the clear copies and recover the system; plaintext is filed beside the cipher, so this is a key-recovery case, not an open text.

title: Sudan Government telegrams with dictionary code words (Aglossa, Agyllinos, Alantapfel, Flagitate ...) left undecoded in the Khedive's copies
correspondents: Sudan Government departments in Khartoum (Intelligence 'Mukhabarat', Finance, Civil Secretary, the Governor-General 'Hakimam') and the Sudan Agency and Finance branch in Cairo
shelfmark: Durham University Library, Archives and Special Collections, Abbas Hilmi II papers, HIL/65/1-1127, e.g. HIL/65/823-824, 849, 910, 928-929, 964, 966, 984, 1030-1031, 1092; also HIL/64 (not listed)
folio_note: Seen as image (cropped contact sheets of 1,024 px frames: about half of each form's text lines). Otherwise clear English telegrams carry artificial code words of a multilingual dictionary code, all beginning A... or Fl...: 'Said Acacio agyllinos sheikh Mohammed Wadai academical agyllinos stop Nuba mountains Mekke Pedura and sheikh Musa el Aisa academical agyllinos' (HIL/65/928); 'ajustamos Yusef Kamel caponarom aginaverid 1913 agitrionne Sunduk Kassala ajelastris' (HIL/65/1030); 'Afrosponde Agazapada to next higher class flamle ... acquisto Hassan Badr ... acquitrino Yusef Kamel' (1031); 'Aglossa 114 flagitate repayment in London' (910); 'Aeruginis floorless to Sirdar' (966); 'all of Alantapfel' (1092). Seen in roughly one telegram in fifteen of the about 265 two-form frames viewed; no decode beside any of them.
status: 15 Nov 2026: code words seen, bare. This is a code book system, not a cipher: reading it needs the Sudan Government's telegraph code (not looked for; the Durham Sudan Archive, TNA FO 141 or WO 33 are the likely places) or a reconstruction from context (the words stand for stock phrases such as ranks, classes of decoration, 'with reference to my telegram'). The A... and Fl... words look like vocabulary of the Berne Official Vocabulary family used by private codes; not checked against any printed code. Count is an estimate from cropped sheets, not a tally. known.py: no hit.
why: Explains what the Durham catalogue means by 'use of code' in HIL/64 and HIL/65. A weak cipher target on its own (stock phrases, partly guessable), listed so the code book can be looked for; with it every code word in the two files reads at once.
verify: Look for the Sudan Government telegraph code book (Durham Sudan Archive, TNA FO 141, WO 33); tally the code words over all frames.

title: Numeral cryptogram of the reader Ioannes after his dedicatory note in a Greek Gospel lectionary (Trinity College O.4.22, f. 248v)
correspondents: Ioannes, anagnostes (reader), saluting his teacher, arch-priest and cousin, whose name the cryptogram is thought to hide
shelfmark: Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.4.22 (James 1253; Gregory-Aland l 186), f. 248v
folio_note: Seen as image (CUDL IIIF, 1,305 x 2,000 px download; page image 503). At the foot of column 2, after the note 'Ego Ioannes anagnostes cheritizo ton didaskalon mou, archierea kai exadelphon mou', three faint lines of capitals. CUDL (Christopher Wright) transcribes: 'ΑΒ· Β· Κ· Β· Γ Ι· Δ ΛΕ ΙΗ· Ϛ ζ: Ζ ΚΖ· Η ΙΕ Θ Δ ΙΚ Δ. ΙΑ· ΙΒ ΙΒ· Α ΙΓ ΚΑ· ΙΑ Θ ΙΕ ΚΘ ΙϚ ΙΖ· ΙΖ Ε ΙΗ. ΚΕ· ΙΘ ΙΓ', i.e. about 40 letter-numerals. The run may pair a running count (1, 2, 3 ... 19) with a value each; not tested. At this size the letters are too faint to check the transcription; a larger download (the page is 4,797 x 7,350 px) is needed.
status: 15 Nov 2026: CUDL record: the text 'appears to have been encoded using a numerical cryptographic system ... is not, however, decipherable by any of the more common Greek cryptographic systems, and remains to be resolved'. One web search for a published solution found none. known.py: no hit. Not searched: Pinakes bibliography for the manuscript, the literature on Byzantine scribal cryptography (Gardthausen; Mioni). Outside the Arabic scope of this sweep; found through the CUDL search.
why: A named cataloguer states that the standard Greek systems fail. Short (about 19 values if the count-and-value reading holds), with a strong expectation of content (a personal name and perhaps a title), and the image is free online.
verify: Download f. 248v at full size (4,797 x 7,350 px) and check the CUDL transcription; search Pinakes and the Byzantine cryptography literature (Gardthausen, Mioni).

title: Coded scribe's or place name in the colophon of a Jain manuscript (Abhayadeva's Vipakasutravrtti, CUL Add. 2255, f. 19v)
correspondents: an unnamed Jain scribe; later owner Pandit Vimalavijayagani
place: Western India (Gujarat or Rajasthan); not stated
language: Sanskrit and Prakrit; colophon note in Gujarati
shelfmark: Cambridge University Library, MS Add. 2255, f. 19v, line 14
folio_note: Seen as image (CUDL IIIF, 2,000 px wide; page image 40). After 'samvat 1650 varse ... kalyanam astu' and before 'lasitam' (= likhitam) stand about a dozen signs in two or three groups divided by dandas, unlike the Jaina Devanagari of the text; they look like numeral forms. The owner's note follows in clear.
status: 15 Nov 2026: CUDL record: the name is 'written in what seems to be coded characters instead of ordinary Jaina Devanagari. Their meaning is yet to be deciphered'. known.py: no hit. No prior-art search (Indian numeral-syllable ciphers such as ankapalli and the scribal 'mula-deviya' substitutions are the obvious first tests). Outside the Arabic scope of this sweep; found through the CUDL search.
why: Stated unread by the cataloguer and on a free image, but only about twelve signs: solvable only if it is a known Indian scribal cipher, which is likely.
verify: Search prior art on Jain scribal ciphers; test the known Indian numeral-syllable substitutions on the dozen signs.
